idiom_name: buffered reply chan + select on ctx.Done()
implementation_notes: Go's channel is the per-request reply channel: the caller allocates a buffered channel, hands it to the request, and selects between the reply and the context's Done channel, so context.WithTimeout supplies the deadline and cancellation instead of a correlation table. The classic structure is only rebuilt when replies arrive on a shared connection: then one reader demultiplexes by request id into a map of channels, or a client library does it - nats.go's Conn.Request allocates an inbox subject, subscribes, publishes and waits with a timeout, returning nats.ErrTimeout when nothing arrives.
pitfalls: An unbuffered reply channel lets a timed-out caller block the replier forever; buffer it by one or have the replier select on ctx.Done() too.
time.After allocates a timer that cannot be collected before it fires - prefer context.WithTimeout or a time.Timer that is stopped in hot paths.
The context deadline cancels only the wait: unless the request carries the same deadline, the replier keeps working on an abandoned request.

variants.name: NATS request with an inbox subject and timeout
variants.implementation_notes: nats.go's Conn.Request(subj, data, timeout) creates a fresh inbox subject, subscribes to it, publishes the request with the reply subject and returns the matching message or nats.ErrTimeout; RequestWithContext ties the wait to a context deadline, and RequestMsg lets the request carry headers. Use it when a broker is already in the stack: it removes the per-call plumbing but adds a broker dependency and hides the reply subject from the application.
pitfalls: One connection multiplexes every request and reply on a single socket, so unlimited in-flight requests share the subscription map - bound concurrency yourself.
The inbox subscription lives only for the duration of the request: a connection drop mid-call looks like a timeout unless connection status is checked.
